card.title: Current-Voltage Relations: Ohmic and Non-Ohmic Resistance

rows.label: Concept
rows.text: **Ohmic conductors** — metals at steady temperature, manganin, constantan — give a straight I–V line through the origin: R = V/I constant. **Non-ohmic** conductors bend the graph: a filament lamp's resistance rises as current heats it; a diode conducts only in forward bias beyond a knee; thermistors' resistance falls with temperature. The graph is the test, and self-heating is the usual cause of curvature.…

rows.label: Formula
rows.text: - Ohmic: I = V/R (R constant) - Dynamic resistance: r = dV/dI - Filament: R ∝ T (roughly)

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: Ohm's Law Validity: Ohm's law $V = IR$ holds only for ohmic materials at constant temperature and other physical conditions. It is NOT a fundamental law of nature but an empirical observation valid for many conductors.  ·  Dynamic vs Static Resistance: For non-ohmic devices, static resistance $R = V/I$ (at a point) differs from dynamic resistance $r_d = dV/dI$ (slope of V-I curve). The dynamic resistance is what matters for small-signal AC analysis.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: "Conductors whose I–V graph is a straight line through the origin obey Ohm's law; others are non-ohmic."

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: ***Diode*** — forward knee ~0.7 V; reverse blocking: the extreme non-ohmic device.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: **The I–V graph is the test:** straight through the origin = ohmic; any bend = non-ohmic.  ·  **A glowing filament is non-ohmic** — self-heating changes R.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: ## 1. Topic Introduction — Straight Lines and Curves Plot current against voltage: a metal wire gives a straight line, a diode gives a kinked curve, a bulb's filament bends downward. The shape of the I–V graph sorts conductors into **ohmic** and **non-ohmic** — and reveals where Ohm's law ends.  ·  ## 2. Fundamental Concepts ### 2.1 Ohmic conductors An **ohmic conductor** obeys Ohm's law: I ∝ V at constant temperature, giving a **straight I–V line through the origin**. R = V/I is constant. Examples: metals at steady temperature, manganin, constantan (alloys with tiny temperature coefficients).…

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: "Draw both graphs side by side; label the diode knee."

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: **Reasoning (2m): Why does a filament lamp's I–V curve flatten at high voltage?** — Higher current heats the filament; rising temperature raises resistance, so current grows less than proportionally — the curve bends toward the V axis.

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: Mention manganin/constantan as ohmic standard-resistor alloys.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: **Self-heating is the usual culprit** — current changes temperature changes resistance.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: Ohmic: I–V straight line, R constant. Non-ohmic: lamp, diode, thermistor.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Thermistors exploit non-ohmic behaviour deliberately — falling resistance with temperature makes them thermometers.

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: **The two-part Ohm's law test** | Condition | What to check | Failure example | |---|---|---| | Straight line | I ∪ V at fixed T | filament, thermistor | | Through the origin | I = 0 when V = 0 | diode (threshold), rectifier | | Constant temperature | re-measure gives same line | wire that heats under test | | Same R both directions | reverse the battery | diode,…  ·  **I–V graph vocabulary** | Term | Meaning | Units | |---|---|---| | Slope of I–V | conductance G = 1/R | siemens (S) | | V/I at a point | static resistance | Ω | | dV/dI at a point | dynamic resistance | Ω | | Equal slopes both ways | symmetric, ohmic | — |  ·  ### Deep dive: why the origin matters The defining test for ohmic behaviour is not just a straight I–V graph — the line must pass through the *origin*, so that zero voltage gives zero current and the ratio $V/I$ is the same constant everywhere.…

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Temperature Must Be Constant: Ohm's law assumes temperature stays constant. As current flows, Joule heating ($I^2R$) raises temperature, changing resistance — this is why filament lamps are non-ohmic.  ·  No verified PYQ; NEB-style practice (graphs and comparisons 2–3m).  ·  Why is manganin used for standard resistors?
